title: General Liability Insurance Cost for Contractors
description: General liability insurance cost for contractors in 2026: monthly ranges by trade, what sets your premium, and how to compare quotes.

body:
General liability insurance for a small contractor most often costs about $40 to $150 a month in the US, and higher risk trades pay well above that. Insureon market data puts construction businesses near $89 a month on average and renovation firms near $94 a month, while painters sit near $59 a month and roofers near $267 a month. Treat every figure here as a market range, not a quote: your premium is set by your trade, your state, your revenue and your claims history.

## What contractors pay in 2026: market ranges by trade

The table below pulls monthly averages reported by Insureon and summarized from Insureon data. Annual figures are the annual figures the sources list, or the monthly figure times 12 where a source lists monthly only. All are for standard limits of $1 million per occurrence and $2 million aggregate unless noted.

| Trade or firm type | Average per month | About per year |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Painter | $59 | $708 |
| Electrician | $57 | $684 |
| Masonry contractor | $88 | $1,055 |
| Carpenter | $85 | $1,020 |
| Construction business (general) | $89 | $1,069 |
| Renovation and remodeling firm | $94 | $1,124 |
| Plumber | $115 | $1,380 |
| General contractor | $142 | $1,704 |
| Roofer | $267 | $3,204 |

Read the spread, not just the middle. A painter at $59 a month and a roofer at $267 a month both hold the same standard limits. The gap is risk: work at height, heavier property damage claims and costlier injury claims price into the roofing premium. State moves the number too. Insureon reports general contractors paying an average of $144 a month for general liability in California and $84 a month in Michigan for the same line of cover. HomeGuide pricing guidance for concrete work lists general liability at $1,500 to $5,000 a year as an overhead line for larger operations, which fits the top of the range above once crew size and revenue grow. Build this cost into your rates with our [contractor hourly rate calculator](/blog/contractor-hourly-rate-calculator/) so it lands in your price, not in your profit.

## Worked example: budgeting a year of cover for a small remodeling firm

Say you run a two-person remodeling firm and your broker quotes general liability at the Insureon renovation average of $94 a month, listed by Insureon as about $1,124 a year. You also price the two add-ons most remodelers end up buying.

- General liability: $94 a month, about $1,124 a year (Insureon annual figure)
- Tools and equipment cover: $41 a month as an average for installation businesses at Insureon, so $41 x 12 = $492 a year
- Total for these two lines: $1,124 + $492 = $1,616 a year

Now test a second quote for the same limits that comes in at $110 a month for general liability alone: $110 x 12 = $1,320 a year. The gap on that one line is $1,320 - $1,124 = $196 a year, every year. Checked the other way, $196 / 12 is about $16 a month, which matches the $110 minus $94 gap in the monthly quotes. Small monthly gaps are real money over a policy year, and they grow when you add crew. If you hire and your payroll rises, expect the premium to rise at audit, since carriers base the price in part on payroll and revenue. Keep the certificate current and send it fast when a client or a general contractor asks. Jobs are lost over a slow certificate more often than over price.

## What sets your premium?

**Your trade and the work you actually do.** Underwriters price the riskiest part of your work mix. A painter who takes one roofing repair a year can be rated on the roofing exposure. List your work honestly and keep high risk side work off the policy or price it in.

**Your state.** Litigation costs, rules and claim patterns differ by state, so the same firm pays different prices across a state line. The California and Michigan general contractor figures above show a gap of $60 a month on the same cover.

**Revenue, payroll and crew size.** More work and more hands mean more exposure. Solo operators sit at the low end of every range in the table. Firms with several crews sit at the high end, and commercial work often demands higher limits than residential work.

**Limits and deductible.** The market standard is $1 million per occurrence and $2 million aggregate, with a $500 deductible common in Insureon data. Higher limits cost more. A higher deductible cuts the premium but puts more of the first loss on you.

**Claims history and years in business.** A clean record and years without a claim help. One paid claim can lift your price at renewal for several years, which is one more reason to handle small damage on site, fairly and fast, before it becomes a claim.

## What general liability does and does not cover

General liability pays for harm to other people and their property: a client who trips over your cord and breaks a wrist, a ladder that falls and cracks a counter, water damage to a room below your work. It also covers legal defense for covered claims, which can matter as much as the claim itself.

It does not pay to fix your own bad work, it does not cover your own injuries, and it does not replace workers compensation, commercial auto or tools cover. Most contractors end up with a small stack: general liability first, then workers compensation once they hire, commercial auto for work trucks, and tools cover for gear that rides in the truck. A business owner policy bundles general liability with property cover and can cost less than buying the parts apart. Insureon lists a business owner policy at $130 a month for renovation firms and $125 a month for masonry firms, against $94 and $88 a month for general liability alone. Compare the bundle on your own quotes. If you are setting prices now, our [handyman pricing calculator](/blog/handyman-pricing-calculator/) shows how fixed costs like insurance sit inside a minimum charge.

## How to get a fair quote and pay less without cutting cover

Get three quotes on the same facts: same limits, same deductible, same revenue and payroll figures, same work description. A quote built on lower stated revenue looks cheap until the year-end audit bills you for the difference. Ask each carrier what work is excluded, since a low price with your main trade excluded is no cover at all.

Then work the levers that do not cut protection. Bundle lines with one carrier where the bundle truly costs less. Pay the year in full if the discount beats your cost of cash. Keep your claims record clean with basic site habits: cords taped or covered, ladders tied off, drop cloths down, and a quick photo record at the start of each job. Tell your broker when your work mix changes, in either direction. Dropping a high risk service you no longer offer is a fair reason to ask for a re-rate. Review the policy once a year against your real revenue and crew, and check that your margin still carries it using the math in our guide to [contractor profit margin](/blog/contractor-profit-margin/).

## Frequently asked questions

### How much is general liability insurance for a solo contractor?
Most solo, low risk trades land between $40 and $90 a month for $1 million per occurrence and $2 million aggregate limits. Insureon averages put painters at $59 a month and electricians at $57 a month, while higher risk solo trades pay more.

### Why do roofers pay so much more than painters?
Risk. Insureon data summarized by trade puts roofers near $267 a month against $59 a month for painters, about 4.5 times as much. Falls and property damage claims cost more, and the premium follows the claim record of the trade.

### What limits do clients and general contractors ask for?
The standard ask is $1 million per occurrence and $2 million aggregate, which is also the average policy in Insureon data, often with a $500 deductible. Commercial jobs may ask for higher limits, and the higher limit raises your premium.

### Does general liability cover my tools or my own injuries?
No. It covers injury and property damage to others, plus legal defense on covered claims. Tools need tools and equipment cover, about $41 a month in Insureon installation data, and your own injuries fall under workers compensation or health cover, not liability.

### Can I work without general liability insurance?
Some states and licenses require it, and many clients, landlords and general contractors require a certificate before you start, whatever the law says. Working bare also puts your business and personal assets behind every accident on site. At $57 to $94 a month for many trades, it is cheap cover for the risk it removes.
